body.heading: Your body runs on a roughly 24-hour clock
paragraphs: Inside you is a circadian rhythm: a roughly day-long cycle that influences sleepiness, alertness, body temperature and much more. It does not run perfectly on its own. It takes cues from the world to stay in step with the actual day, and the strongest of those cues is light.

Bright light in the morning tells the clock “this is the start of the day,” which helps set the timing for feeling sleepy roughly fourteen to sixteen hours later. In this way, tonight’s sleep is partly decided by this morning’s light.

body.heading: Get outside if you can
paragraphs: Outdoor light, even on a cloudy day, is far brighter than typical indoor lighting. A walk to the shop, a few minutes in the garden, or breakfast by the brightest window all count. Ten to thirty minutes is a common-sense target, not a prescription — more on bright days is unnecessary, and you never need to look at the sun.

If mornings are dark in winter or your schedule is unusual, do the best your life allows: brightest rooms, lights on fully while you get ready, and light as early as your day permits. Imperfect timing still beats none.

body.heading: Pair it with something pleasant
paragraphs: Morning light sticks best when it is attached to something you like: the dog’s walk, the good coffee taken outside, the walk to the station. Habits built on pleasure need less discipline than habits built on duty.
Give it a week or two before judging. Body clocks move like large ships — slowly, and then noticeably. Many people find waking gets a little easier before they can say exactly why.

takeaway: Step into morning light most days, and let your body clock do the rest.
